reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A neurosurgical emergency caused by compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus, requiring rapid recognition and decompression
Classic features include bilateral sciatica, saddle (perineal) sensory loss, bladder and bowel dysfunction, and lower limb weakness
Urinary symptoms progress from difficulty voiding and reduced sensation to painless retention with overflow incontinence, a late and ominous sign
Reduced anal tone and impaired perineal sensation on examination support the diagnosis and should be specifically sought
Because it involves nerve roots rather than the cord itself, signs are typically lower motor neuron with areflexia and flaccid weakness
The most common cause is a large central lumbar disc herniation, but tumour, epidural abscess, haematoma, and trauma are important alternatives
Urgent MRI of the whole lumbosacral spine is the investigation of choice to confirm and localise the compression
Early surgical decompression offers the best chance of preserving bladder, bowel, and sexual function and neurological recovery
reference.pathophysiology: Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of the bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots within the spinal canal below the termination of the spinal cord. Because these are peripheral nerve roots, compression produces lower motor neuron deficits, radicular pain, and disruption of the sacral parasympathetic and somatic supply to the bladder, bowel, and perineum. Sustained compression causes ischaemia and mechanical injury to the roots, and delayed relief risks irreversible loss of sphincter and sexual function.
additionalDifferentials: Acute transverse myelitis or other myelopathy
Peripheral polyneuropathy such as Guillain-Barre syndrome
Spinal cord or vertebral metastatic disease
additionalInvestigations: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine to identify the site and cause of compression
CT myelography when MRI is contraindicated or unavailable
Post-void residual bladder volume measurement or bladder scan to assess retention
Assessment of anal tone and perineal sensation as part of the neurological examination
Investigations directed at the underlying cause, such as inflammatory markers when abscess is suspected
redFlags: New urinary retention, overflow incontinence, or loss of bladder/bowel control demanding emergency imaging and surgical decompression
Saddle anaesthesia and reduced anal sphincter tone
Bilateral leg pain, weakness, or numbness with sphincter disturbance
Fever and severe back pain suggesting an epidural abscess requiring urgent intervention
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on the speed of diagnosis and decompression. Surgery performed before the onset of established urinary retention gives the best functional results, whereas delayed treatment is associated with persistent bladder, bowel, sexual, and motor deficits. Some residual dysfunction is common even after timely surgery in severe cases.
pitfalls: Dismissing back pain with subtle urinary or perineal symptoms and missing the diagnosis until retention is established
Delaying MRI or specialist referral, forfeiting the window for effective decompression
Failing to examine perineal sensation and anal tone
Assuming normal voiding excludes the syndrome without checking post-void residual volume
management: Emergency surgical decompression (discectomy or laminectomy) without delay to relieve compression of the lumbosacral roots
Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine to localise the level and cause and guide operative planning
Cause-directed treatment: evacuation of epidural haematoma, drainage plus antibiotics for abscess, or tumour-directed surgery, radiotherapy and corticosteroids
Bladder management with catheterisation for retention pending and following decompression
Analgesia and, where a compressive tumour or inflammatory cause is present, corticosteroids
Rehabilitation with physiotherapy and bladder, bowel and sexual-function retraining and support
Immediate escalation for progressive neurological deficit or evolving painless retention, and multidisciplinary follow-up across spinal surgery, urology and rehabilitation
